mean: to deal with or have regular contact with someone
lit: to 'do' contact with someone: to have dealings

use.how: Intransitive: the other party comes before it with 跟/和/与: 跟客户打交道. Aspect and duration go inside: 打过交道, 打了十年交道. Can also take things: 跟数字打交道.

near.diff: 来往 is visiting and keeping in touch socially; 打交道 is having dealings with someone, often for work, and can also be used of things like machines or figures.

cue: A friend in customer service says the hardest part of her job is having to handle demanding clients on the phone all day. What does she have to do with them?

ctx.s: 我不太会跟陌生人{打交道}。
ctx.en: I'm not very good at dealing with strangers.

ctx.s: 做销售每天都要和各种各样的客户{打交道}。
ctx.en: In sales you have to deal with all kinds of customers every day.

ctx.s: 我们和这家公司{打过好几次交道}，他们很守信用。
ctx.en: We've had dealings with this company several times; they keep their word.

ctx.s: 当会计的整天跟数字{打交道}，难免觉得枯燥。
ctx.en: Accountants spend all day working with numbers, so it's bound to feel dull at times.

ctx.s: “你跟老王熟吗？”“熟，我们{打了十几年交道}了。”
ctx.en: "Do you know Lao Wang well?" "Yes, we've been dealing with each other for over ten years."

ctx.s: 听说新来的经理不好{打交道}，你跟他说话小心点。
ctx.en: I hear the new manager is hard to deal with, so be careful how you talk to him.

bad.s: 我昨天{打交道}了我的新同事。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I got to know my new colleague)
bad.why: It takes no object: the person goes before it with gen ('with'), as in 'I have had dealings with my new colleague'.

bad.s: 两个孩子在操场上{打交道}，老师赶紧把他们拉开了。
bad.en: (meant: two children were fighting in the playground)
bad.why: Da here does not mean hitting: the expression is about having dealings with someone, not a fight. Fighting is da jia.

mean: to beat around the bush instead of saying it directly
lit: to go round the bends instead of taking the straight road

use.how: Used of talk, usually as a complaint or negated: 别绕弯子了, 我就不绕弯子了. Can be split: 绕了半天弯子, 绕着弯子问.

near.diff: 卖关子 holds back the key part on purpose to build suspense; 绕弯子 avoids saying the point directly, often out of awkwardness or tact.

cue: Your flatmate talks for ten minutes about the weather and the rent before finally asking to borrow your car. What do you tell them to stop doing?

ctx.s: 有话直说，别{绕弯子}了。
ctx.en: If you've got something to say, say it. Stop beating around the bush.

ctx.s: 我就不{绕弯子}了，这次来是想跟您借点钱。
ctx.en: I'll get straight to the point: I've come to ask if I could borrow some money from you.

ctx.s: 你{绕了这么大一个弯子}，原来就是想让我帮你搬家啊？
ctx.en: You went all round the houses just to ask me to help you move?

ctx.s: 她说话从来不{绕弯子}，这一点我很欣赏。
ctx.en: She never beats around the bush, and I really appreciate that about her.

ctx.s: 他不好意思直接问工资，就{绕着弯子}向同事打听。
ctx.en: He was too embarrassed to ask about pay outright, so he sounded out his colleagues in a roundabout way.

ctx.s: 领导批评人喜欢{绕弯子}，新员工常常听不出自己挨了批评。
ctx.en: The boss criticises people so indirectly that new staff often don't realise they've been told off.

bad.s: 他{绕弯子}了这个问题。
bad.en: (meant: he dodged this question)
bad.why: It takes no object. Say he beat around the bush on this question, or, for dodging it, use a verb meaning 'avoid'.

bad.s: 魔术师故意{绕弯子}，等到最后才揭晓答案，观众都很期待。
bad.en: (meant: the magician kept the audience in suspense until the end)
bad.why: Deliberately holding back the key moment to build suspense is mai guanzi; this one means failing to say something directly.

mean: to keep people in suspense by holding back the key part
lit: to 'sell' the guanzi, the crucial turn of a story, by stopping just before it

use.how: Said of someone who pauses before the key bit while others wait to hear: 别卖关子了, 卖了个关子. Often a light, teasing complaint.

near.diff: 绕弯子 is talking around a point instead of stating it; 卖关子 is knowingly withholding the key part to keep listeners in suspense.

cue: At dinner a friend announces they have big news, then grins and makes everyone guess for five minutes before telling. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 快说结果吧，别{卖关子}了！
ctx.en: Just tell us the result, stop keeping us in suspense!

ctx.s: 爷爷讲故事最会{卖关子}，每次讲到一半就说明天再讲。
ctx.en: Grandpa is a master at keeping you hanging: he always stops halfway through a story and says he'll finish tomorrow.

ctx.s: 先{卖个关子}，等大家到齐了我再公布好消息。
ctx.en: I'll keep you guessing for now; I'll announce the good news when everyone's here.

ctx.s: 这部电视剧每集都在关键时刻{卖关子}，让人忍不住看下一集。
ctx.en: Every episode of this series leaves you hanging at the crucial moment, so you can't help watching the next one.

ctx.s: 主持人故意{卖起了关子}，迟迟不宣布冠军的名字。
ctx.en: The host deliberately drew out the suspense, taking his time to announce the winner's name.

ctx.s: 记者问新产品有什么功能，他笑着{卖了个关子}：“发布会上就知道了。”
ctx.en: When reporters asked what the new product could do, he smiled and teased them: "You'll find out at the launch."

bad.s: 他把这件事{卖关子}了三年，谁也不知道。
bad.en: (meant: he kept this secret for three years)
bad.why: It means teasing listeners in the moment by pausing before the key part, not keeping a secret for years. For that, say 'hid it'.

bad.s: 他在市场上{卖关子}，一天能赚不少钱。
bad.en: (meant: he sells goods at the market)
bad.why: Nothing is sold: 'selling' here means dangling a held-back point. Selling goods at a market is simply mai dongxi.

mean: to let others down at the crucial moment
lit: the chain comes off, as on a bicycle, which then stops dead

use.how: Predicate for a person, team or device that fails when it matters: 关键时刻掉链子, 千万别掉链子. Can be split: 掉了链子.

near.diff: 拖后腿 is holding others back, often over time; 掉链子 is failing yourself at the decisive moment, so those counting on you are let down.

cue: The team's best penalty-taker, who never misses in training, blasts the deciding kick over the bar in the final. What happened?

ctx.s: 明天就比赛了，你可千万别{掉链子}。
ctx.en: The match is tomorrow, so whatever you do, don't let us down.

ctx.s: 他平时成绩很好，没想到高考的时候{掉了链子}。
ctx.en: He usually gets good marks, but he fell apart in the university entrance exam.

ctx.s: 我的电脑偏偏在演示的时候{掉链子}，突然死机了。
ctx.en: My computer chose the moment of the presentation to fail on me and froze.

ctx.s: “这次项目全靠你了。”“放心，我绝不{掉链子}！”
ctx.en: "This project is all on you." "Don't worry, I won't let you down!"

ctx.s: 球队前八十分钟踢得很好，最后十分钟却{掉了链子}，被对手连进两球。
ctx.en: The team played well for eighty minutes, then fell apart in the last ten and conceded two goals in a row.

ctx.s: 每次关键时刻{掉链子}的都是他，大家已经不敢把重要的事交给他了。
ctx.en: He's always the one who fails when it counts, so nobody dares give him anything important any more.

bad.s: 他们俩上个月分手了，感情{掉链子}了。
bad.en: (meant: their relationship broke down)
bad.why: It is not about a bond breaking: it means failing to perform at a crucial moment. A break-up is a relationship that has broken down.

bad.s: 我妈妈总是{掉链子}，不让我出去玩。
bad.en: (meant: my mum always holds me back)
bad.why: Stopping someone or slowing them down is tuo houtui; this one is your own failure at the moment others rely on you.

mean: (of a plan or hope) to fall through and come to nothing
lit: to be soaked in soup, gone soggy and spoiled

use.how: Intransitive, with a plan, hope or deal as subject: 计划泡汤了, 旅行全泡汤了. Also 让…泡汤 and the split form 泡了汤.

near.diff: 打水漂 is money or effort spent for nothing in return; 泡汤 is a plan, hope or arrangement that falls through.

cue: You had booked a beach weekend months ago, then a typhoon closed the airport the day before you were due to fly. What happened to the trip?

ctx.s: 下雨了，我们的野餐{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: It's raining, so our picnic is off.

ctx.s: 签证没办下来，出国旅行的计划全{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: The visa didn't come through, so our whole trip abroad fell through.

ctx.s: 公司突然要求周末加班，我的约会又{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: The company suddenly told us to work the weekend, so my date has fallen through again.

ctx.s: “听说你们那笔生意谈成了？”“别提了，最后一刻{泡汤}了。”
ctx.en: "I heard you closed that deal?" "Don't ask. It fell through at the last minute."

ctx.s: 他本来指望年底能拿一大笔奖金，结果公司效益不好，奖金{泡了汤}。
ctx.en: He had been counting on a big year-end bonus, but the company did badly and the bonus came to nothing.

ctx.s: 他想趁假期好好睡几天，没想到一个电话就让他的计划{泡汤}了。
ctx.en: He wanted to catch up on sleep over the holiday, but a single phone call wrecked his plans.

bad.s: 他考试没考好，他{泡汤}了。
bad.en: (meant: he failed his exam and is finished)
bad.why: The subject must be a plan or hope, not a person: say that his plan to study abroad fell through.

bad.s: 大雨{泡汤}了我们的野餐。
bad.en: (meant: the heavy rain ruined our picnic)
bad.why: It takes no object; the plan is the subject: 'once it rained, the picnic fell through', or 'the rain made the picnic fall through'.

mean: to be stunned and at a loss when something goes wrong
lit: eyes gone foolish: staring blankly in shock

use.how: Intransitive predicate for the moment a sudden setback leaves someone stunned: 他一下子傻眼了, 当场傻了眼; causative 让人傻眼.

near.diff: 一头雾水 is not understanding something at all; 傻眼 is being stunned when something suddenly goes wrong, usually knowing all too well what happened.

cue: You reach the front of a long queue at the airport check-in desk and only then realise your passport is still on the kitchen table at home. What's your reaction?

ctx.s: 考试一开始，他就{傻眼}了，题目全是没复习过的。
ctx.en: As soon as the exam started he froze: every question was on something he hadn't revised.

ctx.s: 他打开钱包准备付钱，才发现里面一分钱也没有，一下子就{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: He opened his wallet to pay and found there wasn't a penny in it, and he was stunned.

ctx.s: 看到房间被弄得乱七八糟，妈妈当场{傻了眼}。
ctx.en: When Mum saw the room turned upside down, she just stood there stunned.

ctx.s: “你怎么站在那儿不动？”“我{傻眼}了，车钥匙锁在车里了。”
ctx.en: "Why are you just standing there?" "I'm stunned. I've locked the car keys inside the car."

ctx.s: 本来以为稳赢，没想到对手最后一分钟进了球，全场球迷顿时都{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: Everyone thought it was in the bag, then the other side scored in the last minute and the whole crowd was stunned.

ctx.s: 搬进新家第一天就停水停电，这让我们彻底{傻眼}了。
ctx.en: On our first day in the new flat both the water and the power went off, and we were completely at a loss.

bad.s: 他是个很{傻眼}的人，常常做错事。
bad.en: (meant: he is a foolish person who often makes mistakes)
bad.why: It is not an adjective for a foolish person; it describes the moment someone is stunned: 'he was stunned at once'.

bad.s: 这个坏消息{傻眼}了我。
bad.en: (meant: this bad news stunned me)
bad.why: It takes no object. Say 'this bad news left me stunned', using rang ('make'), or 'hearing the news, I was stunned'.

mean: to be envious of what others have
lit: one's eyes turn red at the sight of what someone else has

use.how: Predicate for the envious person, about money, success or luck: 看到别人赚钱就眼红; also transitive (眼红别人的成绩) and causative (真让人眼红).

near.diff: 吃醋 is jealousy over a partner's attention to someone else; 眼红 is envy of someone's money, success or luck.

cue: A coworker grumbles all week after a younger new hire gets a bigger bonus and a corner office. What is the coworker feeling?

ctx.s: 看到邻居买了新车，他有点{眼红}。
ctx.en: When he saw the neighbours had bought a new car, he felt a bit envious.

ctx.s: 他一年就升了两次职，不少同事都{眼红}。
ctx.en: He was promoted twice in one year, and plenty of colleagues were envious.

ctx.s: 你别{眼红}别人的工资了，好好提高自己的能力吧。
ctx.en: Stop envying other people's salaries and work on improving your own skills.

ctx.s: 听说她中了大奖，真让人{眼红}！
ctx.en: I hear she's won the big prize. It makes you green with envy!

ctx.s: 这家小店生意越做越好，附近的同行都{眼红}起来。
ctx.en: As the little shop's business kept growing, the other shops nearby started to grow envious.

ctx.s: 这笔奖金数目不小，难免有人{眼红}，你最好别到处说。
ctx.en: That's a big bonus, and someone is bound to be envious, so you'd better not tell everyone.

bad.s: 看到女朋友跟别的男生说话，他{眼红}了。
bad.en: (meant: he got jealous when his girlfriend talked to other boys)
bad.why: Jealousy over a partner is chi cu; this one is envy of someone's money, success or luck.

bad.s: 你的新车真{眼红}！
bad.en: (meant: your new car is really enviable)
bad.why: It describes the envious person, not the thing envied. Say the car 'makes people envious', with rang ren before it.

mean: extremely urgent, needing action right now
lit: the fire is already burning one's eyebrows

story.text: The phrase appears in the Song-dynasty collection of Chan Buddhist dialogues. A monk asks a master, "What is the most urgent phrase?" and the master answers, "Fire burning the eyebrows." The image is of danger so close that it cannot wait a moment.

use.how: Describes a situation, as predicate or attribute: 都火烧眉毛了，你还…; 火烧眉毛的事. Often a reproach to someone who is not hurrying.

near.diff: 临时抱佛脚 is someone's frantic last-minute effort; 火烧眉毛 describes the situation itself as so urgent it cannot wait.

cue: Your visa interview is across town in an hour and the forms aren't printed, yet your flatmate asks if you'd like to watch a film first. How do you describe the situation?

ctx.s: 都{火烧眉毛}了，你怎么还在玩手机？
ctx.en: It's a real emergency and you're still playing on your phone?

ctx.s: 离登机只剩二十分钟了，简直是{火烧眉毛}！
ctx.en: There are only twenty minutes until boarding. It couldn't be more urgent!

ctx.s: 别等到{火烧眉毛}了才着急。
ctx.en: Don't wait until it's an emergency before you start to worry.

ctx.s: “能不能明天再处理？”“不行，客户下午就要，已经{火烧眉毛}了！”
ctx.en: "Can we deal with it tomorrow?" "No, the client needs it this afternoon. It's urgent!"

ctx.s: 公司账上的钱只够发一个月工资，情况已经是{火烧眉毛}，必须马上想办法。
ctx.en: The company only has enough money for one more month of wages; it's critical, and something has to be done at once.

ctx.s: 先处理那些{火烧眉毛}的事，其他的下周再说。
ctx.en: Deal with the really urgent things first; the rest can wait until next week.

bad.s: 他是个{火烧眉毛}的人，做什么都很急。
bad.en: (meant: he is an impatient person who rushes everything)
bad.why: It describes an urgent situation, not a person's temperament. Someone always in a hurry is a ji xingzi.

bad.s: 老板{火烧眉毛}我们，让我们今天交报告。
bad.en: (meant: the boss was hurrying us to hand in the report today)
bad.why: It is not a verb that takes an object. Say the boss urged us, and that the matter was now extremely urgent.

mean: someone soaked to the skin, e.g. caught in the rain
lit: a chicken that has fallen into the soup pot

use.how: A noun for a drenched person, usually after 成了, 淋成, 像只: 被雨淋成了落汤鸡. Light and teasing, often self-mocking.

cue: Your friend arrives at the café after cycling through a sudden downpour, hair dripping and shoes squelching. How do you tease them?

ctx.s: 我忘了带伞，被淋成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: I forgot my umbrella and got soaked to the skin.

ctx.s: 看你浑身湿透，像只{落汤鸡}，快去洗个热水澡吧。
ctx.en: Look at you, you're like a drowned rat. Go and have a hot shower.

ctx.s: 孩子们打水仗，一个个都成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: The children had a water fight and every one of them ended up drenched.

ctx.s: 他划船时不小心掉进湖里，爬上岸时活像一只{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: He fell into the lake while rowing, and when he climbed out he looked like a drowned rat.

ctx.s: “怎么没打伞？”“伞被风吹坏了，我只好当了一回{落汤鸡}。”
ctx.en: "Why didn't you use an umbrella?" "The wind broke it, so I just had to get soaked for once."

ctx.s: 暴雨来得太突然，街上的行人一下子全变成了{落汤鸡}。
ctx.en: The storm came so suddenly that everyone on the street was drenched in moments.

bad.s: 今天晚饭我们吃{落汤鸡}，汤很好喝。
bad.en: (meant: we had chicken soup for dinner tonight)
bad.why: It is never a dish; it describes a person who is drenched. Chicken soup is ji tang.

bad.s: 这场雨{落汤鸡}了我。
bad.en: (meant: this rain soaked me)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb. Use the ba pattern: zhe chang yu ba wo lin cheng le luo tang ji, 'the rain soaked me into a drowned chicken'.

mean: a night owl, someone who habitually stays up late
lit: a 'night cat': a folk name for the owl

use.how: A noun for a person, usually after 是, 当, 变成: 我是个夜猫子. About a habit, not one late night.

near.diff: 开夜车 is staying up on a particular night to finish work or study; 夜猫子 is a person who habitually stays up late.

cue: Your roommate is never in bed before three a.m., not because of work or exams, but simply because that's when they feel most awake. What kind of person are they?

ctx.s: 我是个{夜猫子}，每天都两点以后才睡。
ctx.en: I'm a night owl; I never go to bed before two.

ctx.s: 他是出了名的{夜猫子}，你半夜给他发消息，他马上就回。
ctx.en: He's a notorious night owl: message him in the middle of the night and he replies straight away.

ctx.s: “你早上起得来吗？”“起不来，我是{夜猫子}，上午脑子都不清醒。”
ctx.en: "Can you get up in the mornings?" "No, I'm a night owl. My brain doesn't work before noon."

ctx.s: 自从上了大学，她就变成了{夜猫子}，作息全乱了。
ctx.en: Since starting university she's turned into a night owl, and her sleep schedule is a mess.

ctx.s: 这家便利店通宵营业，专门做{夜猫子}的生意。
ctx.en: This convenience store is open all night and caters to night owls.

ctx.s: 医生劝他别再当{夜猫子}了，长期熬夜对身体不好。
ctx.en: The doctor told him to stop being a night owl, as staying up late all the time is bad for his health.

bad.s: 明天考试，我今晚要{夜猫子}。
bad.en: (meant: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll stay up all night tonight)
bad.why: It is a noun for a habitual night person, not a verb. Staying up one night to study is kai yeche or aoye.

bad.s: 我家有一只{夜猫子}，每天晚上出去抓老鼠。
bad.en: (meant: our cat goes out mouse-hunting every night)
bad.why: It does not mean a cat. The word is a folk name for the owl, and as an idiom it describes a person who stays up late.
